newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore chemical plant faces stiff competition.
newsitem.headline: Singapore chemical plant faces stiff competition.

text.p: Singapore's US$2.4 billion petrochemical expansion project due be operational in April will face stiff competition by the end of 1997 with the completion of a major project in Kuwait, a senior industry official said on Thursday.

"It will have a fairly good start until Kuwait (starts up)," said Alan Hammerli, managing director of Phillips Petroleum Singapore Chemicals Pte Ltd, in an interview with Reuters on the sidelines of a downstream energy conference in Singapore. Phillips is one of several international companies expanding an existing petrochemical plant in Singapore to make derivative products like polyethylene, polypropylene and styrene which are used to make plastic products.
Ethylene output in Singapore will more than double to 965,000 tonnes per year once the expansion has taken place, Hummerli said.

But Kuwait and Union Carbide plan to start up a US$2 billion petrochemical complex by end 1997 in Kuwait which will produce annually 650,000 tonnes of ethylene, 450,000 tonnes of polyethylene and 350,000 tonnes of ethylene glycol.
"A lot of new capacity...(starts up) in a short space of time," Hammerli said, refering to new ethylene capacity being brought onstream.
He said after the Kuwait project, the Singapore plant would face strong competition for market share.
He said the increase in capacity will have a negative impact towards the end of 1997 and would carry on into 1998.
But he said the down trend would not be as severe as in 1991-1992, when most chemical companies reported losses.
